title: The Tenth Guru's morning praise
hook: Jaap Sahib is a rolling litany of the Timeless One's qualities, said each morning after Japji

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala: the valley of year one behind you, the ranges ahead, and your line, wow. Today, year two begins with the first range, the daily banis.

What do people do when one sentence isn't enough? Listen to a best man at a wedding. He doesn't say, my friend is good. He says: loyal, ridiculous, the one who drove four hours at midnight, the one who still remembers your mother's birthday. Love turns into a list. The list speeds up. Everyone laughs, and somebody cries. Sikhs have a morning prayer built just like that, a list that keeps going, faster and faster, because no single word will do. It comes right after Japji.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE ISN'T ENOUGH.` → `LOVE TURNS INTO A LIST.` → `THE LIST SPEEDS UP.`

segments.voice: Its name is Jaap Sahib. Jaap comes from jap, to repeat, to recite, the same root as japna, the steady repeating of the Name. Sahib is a word of respect, the way Sikhs honor a bani. So the title means something like: the honored recitation. Sikh tradition credits it to Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib; it opens a second collection, the Dasam Granth, the book linked with the tenth Guru. In the standard text it runs to one hundred ninety-nine stanzas, and almost all of it is names: qualities of the Timeless One, line after line. Many begin with a small sound, a, which means without. Without form. Without birth. Without fear. Without end. It praises by saying: whatever you picture, it's more than that. The language is a rich mix: mostly Braj, an old poetic Hindi, with words shaped like Sanskrit, and passages in Persian, full of Persian and Arabic words. The meter keeps changing, chhand after chhand, some stately, some so quick the words drum. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, lists the morning banis: Japji first, Guru Nanak's quiet wisdom; then Jaap, the Tenth Guru's praise; then ten short verses called the Tav Prasad Savaiye. The first Guru and the tenth, side by side every morning. Japji thinks. Jaap sings, and keeps moving. Over the next thirty days, it unfolds a few names at a time.
screen: `JAAP: TO REPEAT, TO RECITE.` · `THE TENTH GURU, 199 STANZAS.` · `A: WITHOUT FORM, WITHOUT BIRTH, WITHOUT END.` · `JAPJI FIRST, THEN JAAP.` · then, large: `PRAISE AT PACE.`

segments.voice: If you have a recording of Jaap Sahib, play the first two minutes and let it run; you don't need to follow the words yet, only notice how the lines keep coming and never stop to explain. If you can't play anything, listen to the sounds around you, one after another, without naming them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once at the end.
Jaap Sahib. The honored recitation: Guru Gobind Singh's long, quickening list of the Timeless One's qualities, said each morning right after Japji.
Your line: praise at pace. When one word won't do, the list begins. Year two, under way.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep Nitnem recite Jaap Sahib each morning, right after Japji Sahib, often from memory or from a small prayer book (gutka).
